questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Hiring against a marginal revenue product schedule
questions.learningObjective: Hire until marginal revenue product equals the wage.
questions.stem: Explain why a profit-maximizing firm stops hiring where marginal revenue product equals the wage.

answer.exemplar: A firm hires while each worker's marginal revenue product exceeds the wage, because that worker adds more revenue than cost; it stops at equality since beyond that point cost exceeds revenue, and it never hires where MRP falls below the wage.

questions.explanation: The stopping rule compares each worker's revenue contribution to the wage. Hiring stops at equality because further workers reduce profit.
questions.hint: Compare revenue added to wage paid.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a minimum wage cuts employment
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism of job loss.
questions.stem: Explain how a binding minimum wage reduces employment.

answer.exemplar: A binding minimum wage raises the cost of labor above the market level, so firms move up their labor demand curve and hire fewer workers, creating a surplus of labor.

questions.explanation: Higher labor cost moves firms up the demand curve, reducing hires. Confusing supply and demand is the slip.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Internal rate of return and its weakness
questions.learningObjective: Explain IRR versus NPV conflict.
questions.stem: Explain why IRR and NPV can give conflicting project rankings.

answer.exemplar: IRR is a percentage that ignores project scale and cash-flow timing, while NPV measures absolute dollar value at the cost of capital, so a small high-yield project can win on IRR but lose on NPV.

questions.explanation: IRR ignores scale and timing, NPV does not. Trusting IRR alone is the tempting error.

questions.stem: Ticket #1644 has MRP of 9 and wage of 12 for the next worker; should the firm hire?

options.text: Yes, because MRP is positive.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a minimum wage cuts employment
questions.learningObjective: Summarize the employment effect.
questions.stem: Explain the overall employment effect of a binding minimum wage in a competitive labor market.

answer.exemplar: A binding minimum wage raises labor cost above equilibrium, so firms reduce employment along the labor demand curve and a surplus of workers, unemployment, results.

questions.explanation: Higher cost reduces employment along demand and creates unemployment. Confusing supply and demand is the slip.
questions.hint: Firms hire less at higher cost.
